## Summary

In this project, we explored whether clinical measurements such as age, blood pressure, and cholesterol levels could be used to predict the presence of heart disease. Using the Cleveland Heart Disease dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, we compared three classification models: a dummy classifier, logistic regression, and a support vector classifier. We selected logistic regression as our final model, which achieved an accuracy of 90.2% and a recall of 82.1% on the test set. Although the model correctly classified most patients, it still missed about one in five patients who had heart disease. This is an important limitation because failing to identify patients with heart disease could have serious consequences in a healthcare setting. Our findings suggest that clinical measurements can provide useful information for predicting heart disease, but further testing on larger and more diverse datasets would be needed before considering the model for clinical use.

## Introduction

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are a group of disorders of the heart and blood vessels, and are the leading cause of death globally. According to the World Health Organization, CVDs were responsible for approximately 19.8 million deaths in 2022, which is about 32% of all deaths globally (World Health Organization 2025). One of the most common forms of CVDs is coronary heart disease, which develops when arteries that supply blood to the heart muscle become narrowed. This reduces blood flow to the heart and can cause a heart attack. 

Diagnosing coronary heart disease with certainty requires medical procedures such as angiography, which is an expensive and invasive procedure in which dye is injected into the blood vessels and imaged with X-rays. This captured our interest in whether measurements that are commonly collected in routine medical examinations, such as age, blood pressure, cholesterol, could help to reliably predict who is likely to have heart disease. 

In this project, we ask the following question: **Can routine clinical measurements be used to predict whether a patient has heart disease?**

To answer this question, we use the Heart Disease data set (Janosi et al. 1989), sourced from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. We use the subset collected at the Cleveland Clinic Foundation, which was originally analyzed by Detrano et al. (1989). Each row represents one patient, with 13 clinical measurements including age, sex, chest pain type, resting blood pressure, serum cholesterol, fasting blood sugar, resting electrocardiogram results, maximum heart rate achieved during exercise, and whether exercise caused chest pain. The original diagnosis ranges from 0 (no heart disease) to 4, but for our analysis, we grouped values of 1 through 4 together to indicate the presence of heart disease, while 0 indicates its absence. This allows us to approach it as a binary classification problem. 


## Methods

### Data

We used the Cleveland data from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. Since the dataset does not include column names, we added them based on the documentation provided by UCI, and missing values (recorded as question marks) were read in as missing. The original dataset records heart disease diagnoses using values from 0 to 4. Since our goal is to predict whether a patient has heart disease rather than how severe it is, we created a binary target variable. Patients with a value of 0 were classified as not having heart disease, while values from 1 to 4 were grouped together to indicate its presence. We downloaded the dataset directly from its original source using Python, saved an unmodified copy in `data/raw/`, and stored the cleaned data in `data/processed/`.


```{python}
#| output: false

import pandas as pd
import altair as alt

import requests
import zipfile
import io
from pathlib import Path

# Download the Cleveland heart disease dataset from UCI
url = "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/45/heart+disease.zip"
response = requests.get(url)
response.raise_for_status()

# Create folders if needed
raw_dir = Path("../data/raw")
processed_dir = Path("../data/processed")

raw_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
processed_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Save the file exactly as downloaded to data/raw/
with zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(response.content)) as z:
    (raw_dir / "processed.cleveland.data").write_bytes(z.read("processed.cleveland.data"))

#Loading the dataset
cols = ["age", "sex", "cp", "trestbps", "chol", "fbs", "restecg",
        "thalach", "exang", "oldpeak", "slope", "ca", "thal", "num"]

df = pd.read_csv("../data/raw/processed.cleveland.data", header=None, names=cols, na_values="?")
```

```{python}
#Class propotions for binary class
df['target'] =(df['num']>0).astype(int)
df.to_csv("../data/processed/heart_disease_clean.csv", index=False)
```

### Splitting the data

Before exploring the data, we split it into a training set containing 80% of the patients and a test set containing the remaining 20%. We did this first to make sure that information from the test set would not influence our analysis while building the model.

We used stratified sampling to keep the proportion of patients with and without heart disease similar in both sets. This is important because we want both groups to be represented when evaluating the model. We also set a random seed of 123 so that we can reproduce the same split when running the analysis again.

We used the training data for our exploratory analysis and the model development, keeping the test set separate for evaluating the final model. 

```{python}
#| output: false
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

#Splitting training and test dataset
train_data, test_data = train_test_split(df, test_size = 0.2, random_state = 123, stratify=df["target"])
```

### Preprocessing
 

Before training the models, we needed to prepare the data because the clinical measurements are not all recorded in the same way. For numerical measurements such as age, cholesterol, and blood pressure, we filled missing values using the median and standardized the values so that differences in their scales would not affect the models. For the number of major vessels, we replaced missing values with the most common value and then standardized so that they are on the same scale.

We used one-hot encoding for categorical measurements such as chest pain type, resting electrocardiogram results, and thallium scan results, meaning each category became its own indicator column. We encoded the slope of the ST segment as an ordered category and used binary indicator columns for sex, fasting blood sugar, and exercise-induced chest pain. These preprocessing steps were combined with each model in a pipeline so that the transformations could be fitted within the training folds during cross-validation.

```{python}
#| output: false

#Loading the library

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline


```


```{python}
#| output: false

#Building the transformers
numeric_transformer_cont = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler())
numeric_transformer_discrete = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent"), StandardScaler())
categorical_transformer = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent"),OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"))
binary_transformer = OneHotEncoder(drop="if_binary", dtype=int)

slope_level = [ 1,2,3]
ordinal_transformer =OrdinalEncoder(categories = [slope_level])


#Separating the features
numeric_features_cont = ["age", "trestbps", "chol", "thalach", "oldpeak"]
numeric_features_discrete =["ca"]
categorical_features = ["cp", "restecg", "thal"]
binary_features = ["sex","fbs","exang"]
ordinal_features = ["slope"]
```


```{python}
#| output: false

from sklearn.compose import make_column_transformer

preprocessor = make_column_transformer(
    (numeric_transformer_cont, numeric_features_cont),
    (numeric_transformer_discrete, numeric_features_discrete),
    (categorical_transformer, categorical_features),
    (ordinal_transformer, ordinal_features),
    (binary_transformer, binary_features)
)
```


```{python}
#| output: false

trans_df = preprocessor.fit_transform(X_train)

transformed_df = pd.DataFrame(
trans_df,
columns=preprocessor.get_feature_names_out(),
index=X_train.index,
)
n_new_cols = transformed_df.shape[1] - X_train.shape[1]

transformed_df
```

### Model selection
 
We compared three classification models to see how well the clinical measurements could predict the presence of heart disease. We started with a dummy classifier, which always predicts the most common class. This gave us a baseline to compare against, since a useful model should perform better than simply predicting the majority class.

We then tested logistic regression and a support vector classifier (SVC). Logistic regression uses the clinical measurements to estimate the probability of a patient having heart disease, while SVC attempts to separate patients with and without heart disease based on their measurements.

To compare the models, we used five-fold cross-validation on the training data with scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011). This means dividing the training data into five parts, training on four parts, and evaluating on the remaining 20%. We repeated this process so that each part was used for validation once. This helped us compare the models without using the test set during model selection.


### Evaluation metrics

We used accuracy and recall to evaluate the models. Accuracy measures the proportion of patients the model classified correctly, whether they had heart disease or not. Since our dataset has a fairly balanced number of patients in both classes, accuracy provides a useful overall measure of performance.

However, accuracy alone does not tell us how well the model identifies patients who actually have heart disease. For this reason, we also looked at recall, which measures the proportion of patients with heart disease that the model correctly identifies. We considered recall important because missing a patient with heart disease could have more serious consequences than incorrectly identifying someone as having the disease.

```{python}
#| output: false

#Building model using dummy classifier
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate

#Since class proprtions is balanced, we choose accuracy as our classification metrics
classification_metrics = ["accuracy","recall"]
# The dummy model
dc = DummyClassifier()
# The mean and std of the cross validated scores for all metrics as a dataframe
cross_val_results = {}
cross_val_results['dummy'] = pd.DataFrame(cross_validate(dc, X_train, y_train,
    scoring= classification_metrics,cv=5,
    return_train_score=True,)).agg(['mean', 'std']).round(3).T

# Show the train and validation scores
cross_val_results['dummy']
```


```{python}
#| output: false

#Building model using Logistic regression
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

# The logreg model pipeline
logreg = make_pipeline(preprocessor, LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state = 123))

# The mean and std of the cross validated scores for all metrics as a dataframe
cross_val_results['logreg'] = pd.DataFrame(cross_validate(logreg, X_train, y_train, scoring=classification_metrics, return_train_score = True)).agg(['mean', 'std']).round(3).T

# Show the train and validation scores
cross_val_results['logreg'] 
```

```{python}
#| output: false


#Building model using SVC
from sklearn.svm import SVC


# The svc model pipeline
svc = make_pipeline(preprocessor, SVC())

# The mean and std of the cross validated scores for all metrics as a dataframe
cross_val_results['svc'] = pd.DataFrame(cross_validate(svc, X_train, y_train, scoring=classification_metrics, return_train_score =True)).agg(['mean', 'std']).round(3).T

# Show the train and validation scores
cross_val_results['svc'] 

```


## Results
 
We compared the performance of the dummy classifier, logistic regression, and support vector classifier (SVC) using cross-validation. Table 2 shows the average accuracy and recall scores for each model, along with their standard deviations.

The dummy classifier had an average validation accuracy of 0.541 and a recall of 0, because it did not predict any patients as having heart disease. Logistic regression had the highest validation scores, with an accuracy of 0.831 and recall of 0.758. The support vector classifier (SVC) was close behind at 0.810 accuracy and 0.748 recall. However, its training accuracy was 0.912, noticeably higher than its validation accuracy, which suggests that it may be overfitting the training data.


```{python}

#Combining the cross validation results of three models
pd.concat(
    {
        "Dummy Classifier":cross_val_results["dummy"],
        "Logistic Regression": cross_val_results["logreg"],
        "SVC": cross_val_results["svc"]
    },
    axis=1
)
```

Table 2: Mean cross-validation accuracy and recall scores for the three classification models, including their standard deviations. Rows labelled “test” refer to the validation folds in cross-validation, not the held-out test set.

We selected logistic regression for the final test evaluation because it had the highest cross-validation accuracy and recall of the three models. Its validation performance was also closer to its training performance than SVC's, giving us less reason to be concerned about overfitting. Another advantage is that logistic regression is relatively straightforward to interpret.


```{python}
#| output: false

#Choosing the best model
best_model = logreg

#training the best model
best_model.fit(X_train,y_train)

```


```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, recall_score

y_pred = best_model.predict(X_test)

print(f"Test accuracy: {accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred):.3f}")
print(f"Test recall: {recall_score(y_test, y_pred):.3f}")
```

We then trained logistic regression on the full training set and evaluated it using the test set. The model achieved an accuracy of 90.2%, meaning it correctly classified approximately nine out of ten patients. Its recall was 82.1%, meaning it correctly identified about eight out of ten patients who had heart disease.

Although the model performed reasonably well overall, the recall score shows that some patients with heart disease were incorrectly classified as not having it. This is an important limitation, especially when considering the potential use of the model in a healthcare setting.

## Discussion
 
Our goal was to see whether clinical measurements could be used to predict the presence of heart disease. Based on our results, logistic regression showed that these measurements contain useful information for distinguishing between patients with and without heart disease. The model achieved an accuracy of 90.2% on the test set, suggesting that it was able to classify most patients correctly.

However, the recall score of 82.1% is important to consider. Although the model performed reasonably well overall, it still failed to identify approximately one in five patients who had heart disease. In a healthcare setting, this would be a concern because patients who need further medical attention could be incorrectly classified as not having the disease. This shows why looking at accuracy alone would not give us a complete understanding of the model's performance.

We expected the clinical measurements to provide some predictive information, since they are related to heart health, but we did not expect the model to identify every patient correctly. The difference between accuracy and recall was a useful reminder that good overall performance does not mean the model catches every positive case.

There are also limitations to our analysis. The Cleveland dataset is relatively small, with just over 300 patient records, which makes it difficult to know how well the model would perform on a larger and more diverse population. We also only compared three classification models, so it is possible that other approaches could produce different results. In addition, the dataset does not necessarily represent patients in other healthcare settings.

For future work, we could explore additional models and investigate whether adjusting the classification threshold would improve recall. We could also evaluate the model using data from a different patient population to better understand how well it generalizes. Overall, our findings suggest that clinical measurements can be useful for predicting heart disease, but more testing would be needed before a model like this could be considered for use in medical decision-making.
